doc.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Commissions and how she approaches them
summary: She dislikes commissions that dictate a feature, needing writing to come from personal feeling, as with the Spartacus arrangement for Toots Thielemans.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well when you get a commission to write — I’m just going to skip to this question because after hearing some of your work the other night, I’m wondering — if you get a commission to write something, do people usually give you guidelines? Like we are looking for this kind of thing. And if they don’t, where does your initial inspiration come from?

Well the first thing is, actually I don’t like getting commissions. I know every composer likes commissions, because it means you’re being paid to write. But I put myself through a psychological trip a little bit when I get a commission. Luckily people don’t say to me I’d like you to do something that’s kind of this or that. If they do forget it. It’s over. I can’t. I have had people commission me to write an arrangement of something, for instance “Love Theme from Spartacus,” the Danish Radio Orchestra, he came to me. But then he didn’t tell me how to do it. I knew I was doing that piece for Toots Thielmans. So I took the elements of that song that I loved and I developed them, and the elements of that song which I didn’t love I skirted my way around. So generally the thing that I have a problem is if somebody comes to me and says, “I want a drum feature for me,” or, “I want a piece that features me on flugelhorn.” I’m not the kind of writer who can look at a player and say this person technically can do this and this and this and I want to showcase it. For me music is something that has to be really personal. I have to go back into childhood memories, kind of feelings, I have to really transport myself into an experience to feel motivated to write. Because when I was a child and doing music, I didn’t learn music because somebody had — because I was in school and thought music would be an interesting thing to do or somebody pushed me to do it.
